posts.caption: My sister's husband's cousin came out to the barn last Sunday wearing white sneakers and a confidence I found alarming. He'd ridden once, at a county fair, in 2004. He wanted one quick photo on the big mare for his dating profile. I explained that she's 1,700 pounds, has opinions, and hasn't let a stranger near her left side since the spring of 2012. He walked toward the mounting block anyway. She turned her head, looked at him over her glasses, and lifted one front foot. He took the photo from the other side of the fence. It's a nice picture. Of her.
posts.first: The only person my old mare ever let on without a fuss was my dad, who had never ridden in his life and was terrified of her. He sat up there like a sack of feed, holding on with both hands. She walked him around the yard like he was made of glass.

posts.caption: At 6:15 this morning I walked out with my coffee and found Pudding standing in the driveway, looking very pleased with himself. The gate was wide open. The chain was hanging exactly where I'd clipped it. I have now tried a snap, a carabiner, a second snap, and baling twine tied in a knot my grandfather taught me. He has beaten all of them. The big horses never leave. They just watch him go, like he's running errands for the whole paddock. Today's errand was the feed room door, which he also opened. I've started checking the gate before the coffee.
posts.first: My first pony could untie any knot I learned as a kid. I once watched him work a quick release loose with his lips in under a minute, then stand there perfectly still like he'd been tied the whole time. He never went anywhere. He just liked me to know he could.

posts.quote: Bought a $40 fly mask in April. Found it in October in the back pasture, folded neatly, like he'd been planning to return it.
posts.first: I keep a box in the tack room of everything he's pulled off and hidden. Two fly masks, a bell boot, half a halter and one soft brush he lifted out of the grooming tote. He has never once eaten anything he wasn't supposed to. He just collects.

posts.caption: Saturday was our first schooling show in two years, and I had practiced that test until I could ride it in my sleep. Which, it turns out, so could she. She knew every letter by the second week. By show day she was anticipating every transition about three strides early, very elegantly, with her chin up. The judge wrote 'lovely mare, please wait for your rider' in the margin. We finished eighth out of nine. The ninth horse left the arena at C and didn't come back. I framed the score sheet anyway. She looks great in every photo.
posts.first: At my first show as an adult, I went off course in a walk-trot class. There were four cones. I missed one. The horse knew exactly where we were supposed to go and politely went there, and I spent the rest of the ride trying to look like it was my idea.

posts.caption: The forecast called for a 90 percent chance of rain from Friday night through Monday, and for once it was right. The trail ride with the women from the boarding barn got called off by text at 7 a.m. I said all the right things. Such a shame. Maybe next month. Then I put on my mud boots, filled a thermos with tea, grabbed the mystery novel I've been carrying around since August, and drove out anyway. The rain on the metal roof was loud enough that nobody could talk to me. She ate. I read. We both got exactly what we wanted.
posts.first: My favorite sound in the world is rain on a barn roof with a horse chewing hay right next to me. I've fallen asleep on a hay bale to it more than once. The last time, I woke up with a cat on my chest and no idea what day it was.

posts.caption: When we got married, my husband thought the horse was a phase. He'd stand by the truck in his good shoes while I did chores, checking his watch. That was 2006. Somewhere along the way, I'm not sure when, he started walking out with me after dinner. Then he started going without me. Now there's a paper sack of carrots by the back door that I did not buy, and the old gray nickers when he hears the screen door. My husband swears it's one carrot a night. I've counted the bag. He's never been good at math.
posts.first: My dad called my horses hay burners for thirty years and never once touched one. After he retired I caught him at the fence one morning, telling my mare about the weather and the price of gas. He stopped as soon as he saw me. She kept listening.
